name: Zane Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at Redhill, the big iron ore pit north of town. Twelve-hour day shifts, seven on and seven off, a 220-tonne truck going from the shovel to the crusher and back, maybe forty loads a shift. I like the quiet up in the cab and the radio banter with the crew. What wears me out is the seat, honestly, my lower back after day six.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how are things with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Jess is a nurse at the district hospital, and we rent a house on Station Road. We've got about ten months of my pay put away and the ute's paid off, so we're not stretched. I'm in the union and I go to most of the meetings, mostly because my old man always said you show up or you get walked over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Half the stuff they sold us about computers running the pit was a sales pitch for the board. I'd probably say that in the crib room and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means my life stays about the same, and I'm fine with that. The pay's good, Jess and I are saving for a deposit, and I like my crew. I'm not hungry for change, never have been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving, keep the roster, keep putting money in the house account every fortnight. Maybe do the water cart ticket so I can cover more gear when someone's off. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. The only thing nagging me is my back, and that's the seat, not the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the deposit. How close are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We want about sixty thousand and we're a bit over halfway. If nothing changes at the mine, we buy something small in town in two years. Jess wants a garden and I want a shed, so that's the deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Redhill that already feels routine enough for software to take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pre-start checklist on the tablet, maybe, and the shift reports the supervisor fills in. That's not my bit. My bit is reading a wet haul road at four in the morning, and no app does that.

say: I'd tell the crew the **robot hype** was mostly a sales pitch for the board.
I'd say the pit runs on **people reading the road**, not on software.
think: Privately, I'm **relieved**, because a steady life is exactly what I want.
My **house deposit** stays on track, about two years away, if nothing changes.
do: Keep driving the same **seven-on, seven-off** roster at Redhill and stay with my crew.
Put money in the **house account** every fortnight towards the sixty thousand deposit.
Pick up the **water cart ticket** so I can cover more gear.
feel: Mostly **relaxed**, with my sore **lower back** the only real complaint.
S0.quote: My bit is reading a wet haul road at four in the morning, and no app does that.
fieldNote: He **dislikes change** and says so plainly; a quiet life is the goal, not a fallback.
Secure pay, a **nurse partner** and ten months saved mean nothing here touches his money.
His only routine screen work is the **pre-start checklist**, so AI Plateau barely reaches his day.

steps.text: Keep driving the 220-tonne truck on the same roster
Pay into the house account every fortnight towards the deposit
Get the water cart ticket to cover more machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the companies will use this to squeeze crews, and we need the union in the room before it happens. I'd post that, too. Bellbird next door went driverless trucks in 2024 and nobody asked the drivers anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the desk stuff goes first, the planners and the dispatchers. Robots come slower to the pit, but Bellbird proves they're coming for trucks like mine. I reckon I've got a few years, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go to every union meeting about automation and push for a deal on retraining and redeployment in writing. Keep saving, maybe push the deposit back a year so we've got more cushion. I won't touch the AI tools myself, I'd rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, but I'd be watching every new truck that comes through the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the dispatchers if their jobs shrank first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to come to the meeting and bring their mates. Dispatch is where the company tests things before it tries them on us. If dispatchers lose quietly, we lose loudly later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not touch the AI tools. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust them and I don't need them to drive. My partner Jess uses one for rosters at the hospital and it double-booked her twice. I'll learn what I'm made to learn, nothing more.

say: I'd warn that companies will use AI to **squeeze crews** unless the union is in the room.
I'd point to **Bellbird's driverless trucks**, brought in without asking a single driver.
think: The **planners and dispatchers** go first, but robots will reach trucks like mine.
I reckon I have **a few years**, not forever, in the cab.
do: Attend every **union meeting** on automation and push for a written retraining deal.
Push the **house purchase** back a year to keep more cushion.
Avoid **AI tools** unless the company makes them compulsory.
feel: **Uneasy** and watchful, eyeing every new truck that rolls through the gate.
S1.quote: Dispatch is where the company tests things before it tries them on us. If dispatchers lose quietly, we lose loudly later.
fieldNote: His fear is **concrete**: the neighbouring pit already runs driverless trucks.
He turns to the **union** before anything else, true to his outlook and his father's advice.
Resists the tools himself, citing a **double-booking** his partner suffered at the hospital.

steps.text: Push the union for a written redeployment and retraining deal
Delay buying the house by a year to hold more cash
Watch which new trucks arrive before deciding anything else

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for governments to step in, hard and fast. Tax the robots, fund wages while people retrain. I'd be loud about it, online and at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my truck's gone by 2031, maybe earlier, because Redhill only needs a reason. I'd be thirty-two with no trade but driving. Ten months of savings sounds big until you picture a whole town of drivers looking at the same three jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Jess and plan around her wage, because hospitals will still need hands for a while. I'd stop the house plan and keep the cash. Then I'd go to the union and push for a fight over the transition, and I'd probably look at a trade like electrical, even though I hate the idea of starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the word. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your crew on the first shift after the news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them nobody signs anything on their own, we go in together. Half of them have kids and mortgages, so they'd be worse off than me. I'd be thinking about Davo on our crew most, he's got three kids under six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at electrical but hate starting over. Would you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the union deal falls through, yes, I'd have to. I'd rather fight for the job I've got first, that's just me. But I'm not stupid enough to sit in the cab till the last day.

say: I'd call for governments to **tax the robots** and fund wages while people retrain.
I'd be **loud** about it, online and at the mine gate.
think: My **truck's gone by 2031**, and I'd be thirty-two with only driving behind me.
Ten months' savings shrinks fast when **a whole town** chases the same jobs.
do: Rebuild the **household budget** around my partner's nursing wage in the first month.
Shelve the **house purchase** and keep every dollar of the deposit in cash.
Push the **union** for a transition fight, then start **electrical** if that fails.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing sums about rent and savings.
S2.quote: Ten months of savings sounds big until you picture a whole town of drivers looking at the same three jobs.
fieldNote: Even with **strong savings**, he expects to lose the job outright by 2031.
The three-year gap before robots feels to him like **borrowed time**, not safety.
Resistance shows in the order: **fight first**, retrain only when the fight is lost.
He worries more about **Davo**, a crewmate with three young kids, than himself.

steps.text: Shelve the house purchase and keep the deposit in cash
Rally the crew and union to bargain together, not alone
Enrol in an electrical apprenticeship if the union deal fails
Campaign for a robot tax that funds retraining wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, but with more time to organise. I'd say we've got five years to get a proper transition deal written into law. I'd be at the rallies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to thirty-two before the thinking stuff changes, and thirty-five before robots drive the truck. That's time to get a trade done without panicking. I still think the driving job goes, I just don't think it goes tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrical apprenticeship part-time on my off-weeks within the first year, slow and steady. Keep saving, and maybe still buy the house, but a cheaper one. And keep going to union meetings, because five years is how long a good fight takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one. There's a plan I can actually follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the cheaper house look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A two-bedder on the east side instead of the place near the oval we'd been eyeing. A smaller mortgage means my partner Jess could carry it alone if she had to. That's the test I'd use for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, Dad would get it, he lost a smelter job in his forties and had to start again in the mines. He'd say get the trade done before you need it. My mum would just tell me not to worry, which never helps.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to write a proper transition deal into law.
I'd turn up at **rallies** and say the same thing every time.
think: The truck still goes, but around **2034**, when I'm thirty-five.
That gives me time to finish a **trade** without panicking.
do: Start a **part-time electrical apprenticeship** on my off-weeks in the first year.
Buy a **cheaper house** that my partner could pay on her own wage.
Keep attending **union meetings** for the whole five-year stretch.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier than the fast picture because there's a **plan**.
S3.quote: A smaller mortgage means my partner Jess could carry it alone if she had to. That's the test I'd use for everything.
fieldNote: The extra years turn **refusal** into a **slow plan**, though he still expects to lose the cab.
His test for every decision is whether **Jess's wage** alone could carry it.
His father's **smelter job loss** in his forties shapes how seriously he takes this.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrical apprenticeship on off-weeks
Buy a two-bedroom house Jess could pay alone
Keep going to union meetings on the transition deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to do this properly, so no excuses for governments or companies. Every miner should get a funded retraining place. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039 means I'm forty, and that's a long way off for me. The rosters and dispatch go digital in 2036, but I'd still be in the cab for a while. I'd probably wait a few years before doing anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy the house as planned, keep saving, keep driving. Maybe around 2030 I'd start the electrical ticket so I'm done before the robots turn up. Keep pushing the union to get a retraining fund agreed early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled, with a worry sitting in the back of my head. It's the kind you forget about between meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a few years. What would make you start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my mine ordered driverless trucks, I'd start retraining the next week. That's the only signal I'd trust. The news says a lot of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the younger drivers coming in now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them told straight, on day one, that this job has an end date. Nobody told my dad that at the smelter. Ten years is enough warning if someone actually gives it.

say: I'd say a decade means **no excuses** for governments or companies.
Every miner should get a **funded retraining place**, and I'd keep repeating it.
think: Robots in **2039** means I'm forty, which feels a long way off.
Dispatch goes digital in 2036, but I'd likely **stay in the cab** a while.
do: Buy the **house** as planned and keep driving the same roster.
Start the **electrical ticket** around 2030 so it's done before robots arrive.
Press the union to agree a **retraining fund** early.
feel: Fairly **settled**, with a worry he forgets **between meetings**.
S4.quote: If my mine ordered driverless trucks, I'd start retraining the next week. That's the only signal I'd trust.
fieldNote: With a decade's warning his own income looks safe for now, so he **delays** action.
He trusts **one hard signal**, a truck order at his own mine, over any forecast.
Wants new drivers told the job has an **end date**, from his father's experience.

steps.text: Buy the house as planned and keep driving
Push the union to agree a retraining fund early
Wait for a driverless truck order before anything bigger

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. Three years between the computers and the robots isn't enough for a town full of drivers to retrain at once. What would help is a deal, signed before it hits, that pays us while we learn a trade, and a robot tax to fund it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the towns, not just the jobs. If my mine goes driverless, the pub, the footy club and the school all shrink too. Nobody counts that.

headlineQuote: If my mine goes driverless, the pub, the footy club and the school all shrink too. Nobody counts that.
portrait: Zane is a 27-year-old **haul truck driver** at Redhill, a large iron ore pit, living with his nurse partner Jess.
He has **ten months saved**, a paid-off ute and a house deposit half built.
He dislikes change, never uses **AI tools** and turns first to the **union** when threatened.
He shrugs at AI Plateau, grows watchful in Steady Disruption and is alarmed by AGI by 2028.
With more warning he lays out a slow **electrical trade** plan, tested against his partner's wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years before robots is too short for a town of drivers to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **signed deal** before it hits that pays miners while they learn a trade.
A **robot tax** to fund that pay.
